# Wounds and Trauma
## Trauma types
- [color=#ff5c5c]Ballistic[/color] — deep wound, external or internal bleeding, possible damage to an organ, bone, nerve, and tendon. - [color=#ff5c5c]Piercing[/color] — narrow deep wound with a high chance of vessel or organ damage. - [color=#ff5c5c]Cutting[/color] — open wound with vessel, tendon, and nerve damage. - [color=#ffcc66]Blunt[/color] — bruise, fracture, and internal structure damage. - [color=#ffcc66]Blast[/color] — multiple local injuries and a systemic effect. - [color=#ffcc66]Thermal[/color] — burn or cold injury to tissue. - [color=#ffcc66]Electrical[/color] — local trauma and strain on heart rhythm. - [color=#ffcc66]Chemical[/color] — tissue damage and systemic toxic load. - [color=#ffcc66]Barotrauma[/color] — pressure damage.
## Wound parameters
- body region; - depth and severity; - open or closed state; - capillary, venous, arterial, or internal blood source; - contamination, infection stage, and necrosis; - bandage, hemostatic, pressure, and tourniquet; - healing progress and scar; - foreign body and exit wound.
## Structural damage
- [color=#58e6d9]Bone[/color] — fracture state, stability, displacement, and need for splinting. - [color=#58e6d9]Joint[/color] — stability, dislocation, and movement restriction. - [color=#58e6d9]Tendon[/color] — integrity, movement, and grip. - [color=#58e6d9]Nerve[/color] — sensitivity, motor function, and neural interface. - [color=#58e6d9]Organ[/color] — structural integrity and functional capacity.
## Wound progression
1. Contamination increases infection load. 2. Infection progresses through the stages: contamination, local, deep, organ, systemic, and sepsis. 3. Deep infection creates necrosis. 4. Movement and repeated trauma can reopen a wound. 5. A healed severe wound forms a scar.
For treatment selection, use the [color=#58e6d9]Wounds[/color], [color=#58e6d9]Regions[/color], and [color=#58e6d9]Organs[/color] tabs.
